votes.rationale: I rank purely on how many named vendors are demonstrably cashing named checks for this exact job, sourced to a directly-fetched page. B4 wins: two vendor-owned pricing pages fetched 2026-08-19 — Alt Legal at $60–$295/mo by matter count plus a $30–95/mo watch add-on, and Markify itemising US-federal watch at $39/yr — meaning both the firm segment and the single-mark owner are already paying cash for docketing and collision watch. (Caveat I distrust: the $9–15/mo/mark hypothesis is 3–4x Markify's proven annualised price.) B3 is second on market thickness — VerifyCarrier's own pricing page prices "Carrier Monitoring" as a separate $49/$99/$249 line, and SaferWatch, Carrier411, CarrierOK and Decipher's Freight Shield corroborate; but only one clean first-party price, with the $79.95 and $34.95 figures coming from a broker blog and a competitor's comparison page, and the TIA $700M–$1B figure self-flagged as secondary. B2 third: a federal must-do plus ExclusionScreening's $30/$40 tiers (search-fetched, not direct) and first-party $780/revalidation and $600–2,400/provider/yr credentialing prices — real money, but the lead tier's clearing price is tiny. B1 fourth: strongest Andreessen pull (11 Sep 2026, €15M) but that is coercion, not revealed behaviour; the paid proof is adjacent (sbomify $159/mo artifact hub, FOSSA $20/project). B8's true comp, Red Flag Alert £200/mo, is a Capterra listing, not the vendor, and Inform Direct's money buys filing, not monitoring; an unverified free Companies House alert may serve the job at £0. B7 has one real $199 Gumroad check but free incumbents and a buyer mismatch. B6 names a paying vendor (GridTracker) without a price and asserts WTP. B5 cites no competitor price at all — pure hypothesis.

Through the speed-to-first-charged-card lens, B2 wins: one live-fetched 15.5MB LEIE CSV (HTTP 200, columns confirmed 2026-08-19), zero customer-side integration (paste a roster), pure string/NPI matching with no generative step, and the strongest direct proof any buyer here purchases without a call — ExclusionScreening's own fetched pricing page shows $30-40/mo self-serve in this exact segment. Its SAM.gov key is the one gate, and an LEIE-only v1 charges before that clears. B8 is the lightest build in the ballot — no corpus at all, a live-verified free-key API with a documented 600/5min ceiling, a JSON diff as the deliverable — but its WTP evidence is a Capterra secondary listing, and its own card concedes a free Companies House follow-alert may blunt the sale, so demand is softer. B1 has the only hard external clock (11 Sep 2026, EC page fetched), but the buyer must wire CI to emit per-release SBOMs before seeing value, and the ENISA/Art.14 obligation model is hand-authored pre-revenue work — a 3-5 week build overshoots the trigger it depends on. B3 and B4 are small builds with trivial ingestion but both sit behind registration-gated keys; I distrust B3's "free and keyless" QCMobile claim and note it self-flags UCR/Socrata cadence as unverified, while B4's statutory rule table is admittedly still to be pulled from CFR/TMEP and its similarity scorer needs tuning. B7 is deterministic and ungated but demands a 60-quarter, schema-drifted ETL over 250MB workbooks against free incumbents. B6 hits a literal bot wall (PJM 403/503) plus per-ISO tariff rulebooks. B5 is last on its own admission: 5-7 weeks, six CMS sources, .MDB ingest, and an unresolved AMA CPT licensing question before a line of code.

B8 wins outright: one source (Companies House REST API, verified live 401 = real endpoint, free key, documented 600 req/5min), one jurisdiction, an exact integer join key (company number), and a paid deliverable that is literally a JSON diff of two nightly snapshots into a template. No fuzzy matching, no rule table, no second feed. B2 is next — two federal CSVs, one matcher, one report, and it degrades to one source (LEIE, fetched live at 15.5MB with named columns) while still delivering most of the value; its fuzzy-name weakness is disclosed as evidence-shown rather than adjudicated, so it does not have to be solved. I discount the SAM.gov leg slightly: a 404-without-key proves reachability, not a working extract. B4's lead tier is one API plus a lookup table, but it asserts a date, so the statutory rule table must be complete — and the card itself concedes the OA window and extension branching are unverified, plus the 60 req/min limit is second-hand; the watch tier adds a whole second bulk XML feed and a similarity function the card admits needs tuning. B7 is one source family and the best-verified evidence on the board (byte counts, content-types), with drift as a one-time batch. B6 falls on seven tariff rulebooks, PJM bot-blocked, and an unsourced claim I distrust — that the public queue xlsx carries per-project milestone-schedule columns. B3 needs five-plus FMCSA feeds, several only "confirmed to exist." B1 stacks CI SBOM generation across every ecosystem, five vuln feeds, and a hand-maintained CRA obligation model. B5 is last: six CMS sources, MAC-jurisdiction modeling, .MDB longitudinal diffs, AMA CPT licensing shaping the UI, 5-7 weeks self-declared.

Judged only on whether the paid artifact is deterministic computation over structured data with the model confined to ordering/drafting. B8 wins outright: exact company-number join key, a nightly JSON diff of typed fields (confirmation_statement.next_due, company_status, PSC notified_on/ceased_on) rendered into a template, with the API live-verified (401 on unauthenticated /company/00000006) and a documented 600-per-5-min ceiling. No model is required anywhere. B2 is next — NPI/name matching over two federal CSVs, LEIE fetched live at 15.5MB with columns confirmed, and the PECOS expansion is a pure exact-key join; its residual fuzziness (LEIE surname collisions) is disclosed and degrades to showing raw rows rather than asserting. B3's lead tier is equally clean boolean diffs on DOT-keyed fields, but I discount it: the UCR Socrata fields were "confirmed to exist" not fetched, CarrierOK pricing and the TIA $700M-$1B figure are secondary, and the chameleon tier adds address/officer entity resolution plus a score customers act on. B7 has the best raw file verification (HTTP 200, content-type, 251,850,891 bytes) but its entire moat is fuzzy employer dedup across 15+ years of schema drift — a silent mis-mapping channel. B6 is a clean xlsx diff on CAISO (376KB OOXML verified) yet carries hand-authored per-ISO tariff milestone rulebooks and a bot-blocked PJM. B4 and B1 lose on judgment: MarkCollide is a bare similarity threshold the customer acts on (the card admits edit distance is inadequate), MarkDocket's own statutory windows are unverified; B1 has an LLM writing the notification narrative plus a maintained CRA obligation decision tree and scope checker — policy interpretation as the product, with the ENISA field schema unsourced. B5 is last: prose LCD diffing, admitted two-reading applicability ambiguity, dollar figures acted on, and the unlinked 475,091-record claim.

Ranked purely on forced budget, reference price, and whether the number holds with zero touch. B1 wins outright: the only hard legal mandate with a dated trigger (11 Sep 2026, EC's own page) and a quantified downside (EUR 15M/2.5% turnover), plus a live-fetched self-serve reference price (sbomify $159/mo) sitting below its $299 filing-artifact tier. Its value metric — versions-under-watch — expands with the customer's own release cadence, the cleanest Ramanujam metric here. B6 is second on price ceiling magnitude, not evidence quality: a lost queue position and broken ITC safe harbor is a seven-figure event for a capital-rich developer, so $99-399/mo is almost certainly under-priced; I distrust the card's GridTracker anchor, which proves a product exists but quotes no price, and PJM being bot-blocked caps launch WTP for multi-ISO portfolios. B5 has recurring, felt cash loss and a good four-times-a-year purchase trigger, but its "five figures per quarter" and AAPC comparison carry no fetched price at all, and AMA CPT licensing constrains what can be sold. B8 has the ballot's best value-metric proof (Inform Direct's own £0.69/company); the unverified free Companies House alert is the ceiling risk. B2 and B3 both invert the lens: each has excellent live-fetched anchors ($30-40 capped, $49-249 monitoring, $79.95 all-in) and then chooses to undercut them — flat-unlimited $49 destroys the roster-size expansion axis; B3's card concedes no moat beyond price. B4 has the best-sourced anchor (Alt Legal $60-295) but deliberately targets buyers defined by inability to pay it, at $15-19/mo against a $39/year watch anchor — below the band zero-touch SaaS survives. B7 last: no forced budget, free incumbents, and a single $199 indie Gumroad one-time as its only anchor.

Through the moat lens only, one question decides it: what does a funded 2027 copycat not get to have? B1 wins on two counts. Its asset is not public data but the customer's own per-release SBOM archive, built in their CI and stored immutably with artifact hashes — a shipped version's dated attestation cannot be reconstructed retroactively by anyone, so every release deepens a lock that also grows the bill (usage-fed expansion). Layer two, the authored CRA Art.14 obligation model and the versioned diff of ENISA/EU guidance, is Thiel-style assembly nobody sells; layer three is textbook Helmer counter-positioning — Snyk/Mend/Sonatype/FOSSA cannot ship $99/mo self-serve without cannibalising enterprise ACVs (FOSSA's own $20/project page, fetched, proves the model). B5 is second: CMS publishes snapshots, not changelogs, so a maintained weekly MCD/NCCI revision history plus each customer's code-mix, MAC and resolved-ambiguity settings compounds, and it counter-positions against reference-library pricing (AAPC). B6's snapshot archive is real but its own evidence refutes exclusivity — GridTracker already sells the complete historical queue dataset via Snowflake share, so the history is purchasable; PJM bot-blocking adds acquisition fragility. B4 has weak data compounding (USPTO daily XML and TSDR are re-crawlable) but genuine counter-positioning under Alt Legal's per-matter floor plus 5-10-year §8/§9 renewal lock-in. B2 I distrust most: the PECOS "moat" claims un-backfillable snapshots while the same card records 40+ monthly CMS CSVs archived back to 2022 — self-refuting; only the customer's dated screening evidence trail locks. B8's lateness baseline is equally refuted by Companies House's own free filing-history API. B3 and B7 concede it outright ("None beyond focus and price"; ETL hygiene against free MyVisaJobs/H1BGrader) — pure re-crawlable public data, no time-lock, no compounding.

Judged only on channels that compound without a salesperson. B7 wins outright: DOL's live-fetched 252MB LCA + 156MB PERM quarterlies (HTTP 200, 2026-08-19) are a natural employer x role x year programmatic surface, and the card's own named comparables — MyVisaJobs, H1BGrader — are themselves SEO-funded freemium sites, i.e. live proof the channel converts here, plus a free lookup wedge, huge B2C search demand subsidising a B2B seat, and an ATS/API listing path. B4 is second: the USPTO daily XML (TRTDXFAP, 200 OK) plus TSDR yields a per-mark page surface and a "is this name taken / when is my deadline" free tool aimed at Amazon/DTC sellers who congregate loudly; Trademarkia and Justia already own much of that SERP, which is the discount. B5 third — it is the only card that writes a Bullseye plan explicitly (free Thursday-drop digest, per-code change-history pages, $149 self-serve entry) — but AMA's CPT licence, which the card itself flags, guts the highest-volume half of that page surface. B1 fourth: GitHub Marketplace plus a free repo NOTICE scanner is a genuine compounding listing, and the live HN Algolia pull (8 stories, up to 215 points) is real evidence of congregation — but that sentiment is hostile, and a 11-Sep-2026 deadline is a spike, not a compounding curve. B3 fifth: loud communities and a huge DOT-lookup surface, wholly occupied by SAFER, Carrier411, SaferWatch. B8 sixth: Companies House SEO is a commodity and the card concedes a possible free CH follow-alert. B6 seventh — interconnection.fyi is GridTracker's own free funnel, and this buyer is reached at conferences. B2 last: OIG publishes a free LEIE search, so the wedge is already given away, and no channel is named anywhere in the card. The free-tool and community claims in B1, B3 and B5 are all unsourced plans, not observed traction.

Judged purely on how underserved the named segment is at the named price. B1 wins: the 11 Sep 2026 CRA obligation (EC page, live-fetched) manufactures a segment that has no self-serve incumbent — the only self-serve comp found, sbomify at $159/mo, is sourced to its own pricing page and is an artifact hub, while Snyk/Sonatype are sales-led enterprise. That is Thiel's empty category with a dated starting gun; residual doubt is bundling by the SCA giants, not present crowding. B6 is second: the only named comp, GridTracker/Interconnection.fyi (fetched), sells the dataset via monthly CSV/Snowflake share — a data vendor, not a milestone monitor — and the stated alternative is Excel and consultants; I discount it slightly because the cards never test whether each ISO's own customer portal already pushes milestone notices free. B5 third: reference incumbents (Codify, Find-A-Code) genuinely don't sell the inverse, but "nobody sells the inverse" is an unsourced assertion, and free MAC listservs and NCCI edits already bundled into clearinghouse scrubbers are unaddressed free incumbents. B4 has the single cleanest Dunford artifact — Alt Legal's own page (fetched) floors at $60/50 matters, structurally excluding a 3-mark owner — but its watch tier prices *above* Markify's fetched $39/yr, and "no free official reminder system" is unsourced against USPTO's own courtesy notices. B2's per-screen cap into custom quote is a real pricing-page push-away, but the card itself concedes the crowd (ProviderTrust, Verisys) and $40 incumbents cap WTP. B8 fights a free Companies House follow-alert the card admits is unverified, plus bundled practice software; its £200 anchor is Capterra, not the vendor. B7 sits atop free MyVisaJobs/H1BGrader with a $199 Gumroad hobby product as its only price anchor. B3 is last on its own words: "None beyond focus and price," against four funded lookalikes at the identical $49-249 tiers.

Judged purely on recurrence of the job and roster growth. B2 wins because the job is a legally mandated monthly cycle (OIG LEIE "updated by the 10th of every month", live-fetched 15.5MB CSV; SAM daily incrementals) and the deliverable — a dated evidence PDF — is produced every cycle whether or not anything is found, so value never self-terminates; turnover-heavy staffing rosters replenish continuously. I distrust its "$49/mo flat, unlimited roster" pricing: it deliberately deletes the expansion axis Poyar would price on, and PECOS is the only NRR lever. B5 is second on frequency: CMS ships MCD weekly on Thursdays and NCCI quarterly (475,091 records in 2026 Q3 per the card) — perpetual cadence, plus a real expansion ladder (watched codes → NPIs → $799 billing-company multi-NPI tier, "one billing company brings dozens of NPIs"). B8 pairs nightly diffs with a per-company growth axis proven by Inform Direct's £0.69/company. B1 has the best-articulated expansion mechanic in the set (versions-under-watch compounding with the customer's own release cadence, plus the hosted NOTICE page as a switching cost), but the core CRA job is incident-triggered and the 11 Sep 2026 deadline is a purchase trigger that invites post-deadline churn — the card even concedes relicensing events are rare "insurance". B3 is ambient and continuous but competes on price alone with no moat. B6 self-terminates per project at IA execution, and PJM is bot-blocked. B4 loses badly: §8/§9 windows are 5-10 years apart, so a 3-mark owner sees nothing happen for years at $15/mo. B7 is a lookup with quarterly-lagged data whose only direct WTP proof is a $199 one-time Gumroad sale — evidence against subscription retention.

Counting buyers, not TAM. B1 wins on both halves of my test: the pool is every vendor placing digital products on the EU market — tens of thousands minimum — and it is desperate, with a Commission-page-confirmed 11 Sep 2026 obligation date and EUR 15M downside, reached through the most machine-native channel on this ballot (GitHub App install, developer SEO, a free scope checker). sbomify at $159/mo self-serve is a live comparable proving the channel converts without sales. B4 is the pure long-tail play my lens favors: hundreds of thousands of solo/small mark owners at $15-19/mo, with a programmatic-SEO surface (every serial number a page) that is the acquisition channel and the product at once. I discount it one notch because the only watch-price evidence, Markify at $39/YEAR, implies WTP nearer $3/mo than $15; Alt Legal's $60/mo is a firm price, not a solo one. B3 has the ballot's cleanest buyer-at-price proof — a named incumbent publishing $30-40/mo self-serve with a 100-screen cap that literally manufactures the wedge — but sits behind B4 on raw count. B7 has enormous reach and near-zero proven monetization: a $199 Gumroad one-off by a solo seller is not evidence of a recurring recruiter market when MyVisaJobs and H1BGrader are free. B3 (freight) is price-proven via VerifyCarrier's published tiers but capped at a low-tens-of-thousands broker universe with four incumbents; its TIA $700M-1B and complaint-count figures are secondary reporting and I don't credit them. B8 is cheap to build and reachable, but one country and a free Companies House follow-alert the card admits it never verified. B5 is a big universe that collapses to a few thousand billing companies once you accept the card's own concession that practices defer to them, plus AMA CPT licensing. B6 is last on count alone: a few hundred to low-thousand multi-ISO developers, sold by relationship, with PJM bot-blocked.

Through the packaging lens only. B1 wins: the value metric (products × shipped versions under watch) compounds with the customer's own release cadence with no renegotiation, under-counting destroys the compliance value so the metric can't be gamed, the tier boundary sits at a real value step ("does it produce the filing artifact"), feeds are free so marginal cost is nil, the free deterministic scope-checker is a legitimate lead capture against a dated 11-Sep deadline, and the refusal to file kills any success-fee temptation. Anchors are fetched (sbomify $159/mo self-serve; FOSSA $20/project). B8 is second because Inform Direct's fetched £10 + £0.69/company literally proves the market already pays per company monitored — the pricing page is copyable — with Red Flag Alert's fetched £200/mo as ceiling, free API key, and overlapping portfolios amortising polls across customers. B4's metric (marks watched) is ideal and Alt Legal's fetched $60–295 by matter count validates it; one daily XML feed serves every customer at zero marginal cost. I distrust its claim that $9–15/mo "undercuts" Markify's fetched $39/yr — that is 3–5× more, so the watch tier's price does not write itself. B6 has the best margin structure and highest per-unit value but zero fetched price (GridTracker's price is unknown; "high willingness to pay" is unsourced) and $399/mo underprices a queue position badly. B5 has the best free→tripwire→reseller ladder but no fetched competitor price, an unsourced "five figures" anchor, and AMA CPT licensing on the displayed text. B3 is priced entirely by fetched incumbents with the card conceding "moat: none beyond price." B2 deliberately deletes its own value metric — flat fee, unlimited roster, against a $30–40 ceiling. B7 last: per-seat decouples from value, recurring pricing against a $199 one-time and free ad-supported incumbents, with B2C SEO traffic that costs infra and monetises nothing.

Ranked purely by unattended blast radius. B7 wins because its worst unattended failure costs a recruiter a wasted submittal: every field is copied verbatim from a DOL workbook whose live fetch is documented to the byte (251,850,891 / 156,267,808 on 2026-08-19), the cadence is quarterly so a stalled ETL has 90 days of slack, employer-name fuzziness is surfaced as ranked candidates rather than asserted, and the flagged 15-year schema drift fails closed to last-good quarter. B8 is a near-tie: exact company-number join, no date arithmetic (it relays Companies House's own next_due), and the only live-verified documented rate limit in the set (600/5min); docked for nightly-diff false alarms — a partial API response reads as "all PSCs removed" and reaches a credit team. B1 has the best-engineered corpus (CVE-mediated KEV→OSV→purl join, not name matching) and the most explicit fail-closed UNWATCHED state, but the promise "your clock is already running" is precisely a claim outrunning measurement under a 23-day rush. B6 carries a named bot wall (PJM 403/503) plus xlsx column drift feeding wrong-date consequence. B3 stacks the most self-admitted unverified sources — UCR fields unfetched, Socrata cadence unconfirmed, QCMobile rate limit unknown, TIA figures secondary — behind an identity-collision flag with reputational consequence. B2 has the sturdiest pipeline but the worst harm vector: person-level name matching on a common-surname file, plus a keyed SAM.gov feed whose silent expiry is an undetected screening gap. B5's AMA CPT licensing exposure is explicitly undecided, alongside PHI ingest and dollar figures derived from user CSVs. B4 is last: statutory windows the card admits are unverified, 4 req/min document throttling, and a silent poll failure means an abandoned mark.
